records.quote: And then he began chirping his peculiar melancholy song, from which we have taken this history; and which may, very possibly, be all untrue, although it does stand here printed in black and white.
records.paraphrase: The narrator addresses the reader, noting the story may be untrue despite being printed.

records.quote: It's all the same to me," said the Flea. "She may have the old Leap-frog, for all I care. I jumped the highest; but in this world merit seldom meets its reward. A fine exterior is what people look at now-a-days.
records.paraphrase: The Flea reacts with bitterness to losing, complaining that merit is not rewarded.

records.quote: the Leap-frog was a prophet; for that one could see on his back, if there would be a severe or mild winter, and that was what one could not see even on the back of the man who writes the almanac.
records.paraphrase: A claim that the Leap-frog's back can indicate whether winter will be severe or mild.

criteria.rationale: The only near-scientific mention is a whimsical folk claim that a Leap-frog's back predicts winter, presented as fanciful councillor talk, not as materially represented scientific fact, theory, or natural process.
No device, engineered system, or invention appears or affects the fairy-tale jumping contest.
The tale is set in a timeless fable present with no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement.
The story is a moral fable and develops no consequences from an identifiable scientific, technological, social, or historical premise.
The jumping contest is judged by whim and social favor; there is no observation, hypothesis, testing, or evidential revision driving understanding or action.
No other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them appear; talking animals in an ordinary setting do not qualify.
The only misfortunes are a personal loss and a reported death in foreign service, with no large-scale disaster actual, impending, remembered, or causally central.

candidates.description: A world in which fleas, grasshoppers, and leap-frogs speak, possess noble blood and ancient family lineages, and compete in a royal court for a Princess's hand as if they were human courtiers.

novelty.rationale: Anthropomorphic talking animals in a beast fable are a conventional folkloric mode, not a totalizing world-altering difference from the empirical or implied norm. The device is a genre convention (fable/fairy tale) used for satirical allegory rather than an estranging novum that reconstructs the story universe on a systematic new principle.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The talking-animal premise is asserted whimsically without any immanent, systematic account; the narrator even undercuts its truth-value, signaling a fabular rather than cognitive-scientific framing.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The animals-as-courtiers premise does drive the whole plot (the jumping contest and the moral about appearances), but centrality alone does not make it a qualifying novum absent novelty and cognitive validation.

estrangement.rationale: The narrator's direct address flagging the tale as possibly untrue foregrounds the fabular contract with the reader, and the Flea's bitter moralizing supplies satirical estrangement, but this operates as fable/allegory rather than cognitive estrangement.

candidates.description: The claim that the Leap-frog is a prophet whose back reveals whether the coming winter will be severe or mild, exceeding the predictive power of the almanac writer.

novelty.rationale: This is a passing satirical folk-belief asserted by a councillor, not a world-altering difference. It does not reconstruct the story universe and reads as folkloric weather-lore humor.

cognitive_validation.rationale: No systematic or immanent account is offered; it is superstition/folk augury presented for comic effect rather than an imaginary science.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The prophetic-back claim is an incidental aside about the Leap-frog's pedigree and plays no role in determining the plot's outcome, which turns on the jump into the Princess's lap.

estrangement.rationale: The comparison to the almanac writer offers a mild satirical contrast against real-world weather prediction, but has no storyworld consequence.
